implementation_notes: Scala's primary decomposition tool is the trait: it may declare abstract members (the layer's requirements) and concrete ones (its provided services), a class mixes in any number of traits, and the layer's declared type is therefore usually a trait rather than a base class. Member resolution follows linearization (rightmost mixin wins), and a class inheriting conflicting implementations must override and disambiguate with super[Type].member; abstract classes remain the right choice when the layer type needs constructor parameters it must pass on, though Scala 3 traits can take parameters too. Scala 3 also requires a class from another file to be marked open before it can be extended, making the decision to design for inheritance explicit.
pitfalls: Linearization decides which mixin's implementation wins; conflicting members force an explicit override and super[Type].member call, and the wrong order changes behavior silently.
Abstract type members and self-types make a base easy to over-engineer: a layer supertype with complex type members is harder to implement than the layer it serves.
Scala 3 restricts extending classes from other files unless they are open, so a base intended as a layer supertype must be declared open for cross-module members.
